title: Pressure-cooker French onion soup
subtitle: A deeply caramelised soup in under an hour
excerpt: A classic French onion soup built from caramelised onions and rich beef stock. The pressure cooker dramatically reduces the caramelising time, then the soup is finished under the grill with toasted bread and melted cheese.
sourceNotes: Soupe à l'oignon gratinée is documented in Escoffier's Le Guide Culinaire (1903) and appears across French culinary literature from the 18th century. The recipe is common to virtually every French cookbook tradition. The pressure-cooker caramelisation method is an adaptation used widely since the 2010s.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the soup base without the topping for up to 4 months. Add bread and cheese fresh when reheating and grill.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the soup base 2 days ahead and refrigerate. Gratin the bowls to order before serving.

content.text: Proper French onion soup needs properly caramelised onions. Pale, lightly cooked onions give a thin, sweet soup rather than the deep, savoury version the dish is known for. The pressure cooker reduces 45 minutes of open-pot stirring to about 20. It uses a mix of sauté time and pressure to break down the onions.

The cheese-topped bread gratin is served directly in the bowl, oven-safe or grill-safe bowls are needed. For a restaurant-style result, the bowls go under a hot grill until the cheese bubbles and chars at the edges.
Use a good beef stock. French onion soup has very few ingredients, and the quality of the stock is the dominant flavour once the onions are in.

items.prepNote: about 8 large, thinly sliced into half-moons

content.text: Set the pressure cooker to sauté or use the open pot on the hob. Melt the butter with {{olive-oil}} of olive oil over medium heat. Add all the sliced onions and stir to coat. Cook, stirring every few minutes, for 15 to 20 minutes until the onions are deeply golden and reduced to about a third of their original volume. Add the garlic and stir for 1 minute. Pour in {{red-wine}} of red wine and let it bubble for 2 minutes.

Add {{stock-beef}} of beef stock, the thyme, and the bay leaf. Season with salt and pepper. Seal the lid and bring to high pressure. Cook at high pressure for 10 minutes. Quick-release the pressure. Discard the thyme and bay. Taste and adjust the seasoning.

Ladle the soup into oven-safe bowls. Float a slice of toasted bread on top of each bowl. Cover with a generous layer of grated Gruyère or cheddar. Place under a hot grill for 4 to 5 minutes until the cheese melts, bubbles, and chars at the edges. Serve immediately, the bowls will be very hot.

rows.symptom: The onions are pale after 20 minutes
rows.cause: The heat was too low, or the pan was too full to allow moisture to evaporate.
rows.fix: Raise the heat to medium-high and keep stirring. The onions need to be golden-amber, not just soft, this is the step that takes patience.

rows.cause: The onions were caramelised too quickly and retained their sweetness rather than developing complex savouriness.
rows.fix: Add a splash of red wine or a few drops of balsamic vinegar to balance. Longer, slower caramelisation produces a more complex, less sweet result.

content.text: French onion soup is simultaneously one of the simplest and most laborious dishes in the French repertoire, simple ingredients, demanding preparation. The pressure cooker cuts the preparation time meaningfully. The gratin step, which truly cannot be skipped and must be served immediately, is what distinguishes a proper French onion soup from onion broth.
